headline_marked: [[Microsoft open-sources BitNet]] for 1-bit LLMs, enabling 100B params on a single CPU
headline: Microsoft open-sources BitNet for 1-bit LLMs, enabling 100B params on a single CPU
summary: This inference framework allows 1-bit LLMs to run on a single CPU, eliminating the need for GPUs or cloud resources. It promises to process 100B parameter models at human reading speed.
details: Microsoft has open-sourced BitNet, an inference framework designed for 1-bit Large Language Models (LLMs). This innovative framework is touted for its ability to run models with up to 100 billion parameters on a single CPU.

The core promise of BitNet is to remove the dependency on expensive GPUs or cloud infrastructure, allowing powerful LLMs to operate on standard laptops. It can process models at approximately human reading speed, around 5-7 tokens per second.
The project, developed by Microsoft Research, is 100% open source under the MIT License and has already garnered significant attention on GitHub, boasting over 39,900 stars and 3,700 forks.

BitNet utilizes 1.58-bit quantization, a technique where model weights are stored using only three values: -1, 0, and +1. This is a radical departure from conventional LLMs that typically use 16-bit or 32-bit floating-point numbers.
The flagship model, BitNet-b1.58-2B-4T, features 2.4 billion parameters and was trained with 4 trillion tokens. Benchmarks show it performs competitively with full-precision models of similar sizes.

It's crucial to note that existing LLMs like Llama or Qwen cannot simply be quantized to 1.58-bit; models must be trained with the BitNet architecture from the ground up. The 100B parameter capability is currently an estimation from a technical report, with no actual 100B model available for download yet.

While enabling CPU-only inference is a breakthrough, the 5-7 tokens/second speed might be considered slow for real-time applications such as interactive chat or coding assistants. High-speed tasks will likely still require GPU acceleration.

headline_marked: [[Intel CEO hints at return to the memory business]] – says market ripe for innovation, eyes CPU stacking
headline: Intel CEO hints at return to the memory business – says market ripe for innovation, eyes CPU stacking
summary: Intel's CEO suggests memory is no longer a commodity but a strategic asset ripe for innovation. The company is exploring new architectures, including stacking memory on top of CPUs.
details: Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan indicated that new memory architectures are now strategically interesting, a shift from being a commodity business. He views the memory industry as ripe for innovation and has a "pet project" in this area, even hiring former SK Hynix head Seok-Hee Lee.

Tan specifically hinted at exploring ways to stack memory on top of a CPU, noting that this approach could make a lot of sense. He believes there's significant room for innovation in memory architecture that hasn't been fully explored.

Intel originally started as a memory company in 1968 but exited the market in the 1980s due to losses. The company has made several attempts to re-enter or capitalize on new memory types since then, including NAND and Optane, but ultimately abandoned these initiatives.

Re-entering the memory market would require substantial capital for fabs, R&D for competitive process technologies, and time. While memory production is currently profitable, it's unclear how investors would react given Intel's focus on core products and foundry business, and past exits from memory ventures.
